extracted.intended_audience: aircraft engineers, battery/system designers, safety investigators, and technically literate readers evaluating battery choices for aviation
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and selecting battery chemistries, packaging, charging and maintenance practices, diagnostics, and operational limits for aircraft main/backup batteries (illustrated by the Boeing 787 incidents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Battery chemistry suitability / stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of lithium-ion chemistry (Li-cobalt, Li-manganese, Li-phosphate, NMC) affects safety, specific energy, power and life; Li-cobalt is less stable and may be unsuitable for large-format aviation use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page states 'Lithium Cobalt Oxide (LiCoO2) may not be the best technology for onboard aviation' and notes Li-cobalt 'is known to be less stable than other lithium-based systems.' Prefer chemistries with greater thermal stability (Li-phosphate, Li-manganese, NMC) for large-format/aviation use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific energy (capacity) vs application tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: How much energy a battery can store per weight (Wh/kg); high specific energy favors consumer runtimes but may reduce safety and longevity in aviation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 1 lists specific energy ranges (e.g., Li-cobalt 150–190 Wh/kg, Li-phosphate 90–120 Wh/kg). Aviation batteries are often optimized for safety/longevity over raw capacity; Boeing charged cells to 4.025V to reduce usable capacity to ~75% to prolong life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific power (current delivery / C-rate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Battery's ability to deliver current (C-rates); chemistries differ dramatically (e.g., Li-cobalt ~1C, Li-phosphate 35C continuous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design must match required load; Li-cobalt 'should not be charged and discharged at currents exceeding the Ah rating' and manufacturers recommend ~0.8C charge. Higher-power chemistries run cooler and tolerate heavier loads; mismatched C-rate is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cycle life / longevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Expected cycle count and lifespan, which vary by chemistry and are governed by environment and usage (temperature, depth of discharge, load currents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 1 cycle life ranges: Li-cobalt 250–1,000; Li-phosphate 1,000–2,000. 'Life span reflects cycle count and longevity governed by environment conditions and usage pattern.' Prefer chemistries with longer cycle life for aviation systems requiring reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operating temperature range and thermal sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptable charge/discharge and storage temperature ranges and how elevated or low temperatures affect safety and capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Li-ion should not be charged below freezing; fast-charging permissible from 5 to 45°C. Elevated temperature hastens permanent capacity loss; 'Heat is the enemy of the battery.' Design/operations must control thermal environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thermal runaway temperature / thermal stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperature at which a cell goes into thermal runaway varies by chemistry (e.g., Li-cobalt ~150°C, Li-phosphate ~270°C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 1 thermal runaway temps show Li-cobalt becomes unstable at lower temps. Thermal propagation risk requires design measures (dividers, enclosures). The failed B-787 battery reportedly reached ~260°C, causing runaway.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charge limit / recommended cell voltage
rubrics_metrics.description: Maximum charging voltage per cell and how limiting charge (e.g., charging to 4.025V instead of 4.20V) affects life and capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical charge limit 4.20V; Boeing charged LVP10 to 4.025V/cell to prolong life, reducing capacity to ~75%. Guidance: avoid full 100% SOC retention and limit top-of-charge to reduce stress and extend life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charging practices and anti-patterns (trickle/overcharge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper charging regimes: avoid continuous trickle/maintenance charging at 100% SOC; prefer keeping SOC slightly below 100% and recharging at ~80–90%; slow charges preferred over rapid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorrect charging (suspected trickle charge once fully charged) can cause metallic lithium plating and shorts. 'A slow three-hour charge is better than a rapid charge.' Recharge when charge drops to ~80–90%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection circuits limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Battery protection/BMS circuits protect against external faults but have limited effect once an internal fault/thermal runaway starts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The safety circuit 'is unable to stop a thermal runaway once in progress.' Relying solely on peripheral protection is insufficient; containment and chemistry choice are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Containment and packaging (fire- and explosion-safe enclosures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical enclosures and cell dividers to prevent propagation of a failing cell to neighboring cells and to contain thermal events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dividers or metal compartments per cell (Tesla Roadster encases each cell). FAA may require that a Li-ion be allowed to burn out without causing damage—so design must include fire/explosion-safe battery enclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cell-level isolation / internal barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Dividers or compartments between cells to limit thermal propagation during a cell failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recommends 'batteries should include dividers to protect the failing cell from spreading to the neighboring one.' Metal compartments per cell are an effective example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturing quality control and defect rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidence of random field failures due to manufacturing defects (microscopic metal particles, uneven separators); quoted rate roughly one in 4–5 million cells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that rare internal shorts can occur despite quality control. Design and selection must account for non-zero defect rates and include redundancy, containment and detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separator thickness and impurity susceptibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Ultra-thin separators (20–25 µm) increase susceptibility to metallic particle penetration and internal shorts compared with older, thicker designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using thin separators to achieve energy density, increase screening and consider chemistries/packaging that mitigate impurity sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Battery diagnostics and testing limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: No single test captures all anomalies; laboratory stress tests may not reveal field faults; a matrix of diagnostics is needed (EIS, impedance, multi-model testing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page: 'Battery testing is complex and no single measurement can capture all irregularities.' Use multiple tools (impedance spectroscopy, EIS, deep diagnostics, field monitoring) and recognize lab tests may miss rare defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: BMS calibration and state-of-charge learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Battery Management System (BMS) fuel gauge accuracy can drift; occasional deep discharge cycles help recalibrate SOC estimation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An occasional deep discharge is advisable as a learn cycle to calibrate the BMS. Do not rely on BMS accuracy without periodic validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: End-of-life / replacement criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria for retiring batteries (capacity thresholds used for NiCd) may not be sufficient for Li-ion where safety concerns might require earlier replacement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NiCd retired when capacity drops below a threshold; for Li-ion, safety (not just capacity) may set end-of-life. Field use and stress tests must inform replacement schedules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storage state-of-charge and temperature management
rubrics_metrics.description: Storage SOC and temperature significantly affect recoverable capacity and aging; worst condition is fully charged at high temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 2 shows recoverable capacity losses at 0/25/40/60°C for different chemistries and SOCs. Keep Li-ion cool and avoid storing fully charged at elevated temperature; partial charge (e.g., 40%) greatly reduces capacity loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance across ambient extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: How batteries perform in hot and cold conditions: Li-ion typically degrades in cold charging and performs worse than NiCd at low temps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Li-ion should not be charged below freezing; special cell types may allow down to –10°C at reduced rate. Design charging and mission profiles accounting for temperature-dependent behavior and susceptibility to vibration when cold-charged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost vs performance/safety tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturing and materials cost considerations influence chemistry choice; Li-ion cost currently higher than NiCd and lead acid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cost drivers include materials and complex assembly plus protection circuitry. Balance cost with required safety and performance; heavier NiCd may increase weight and count but could be cheaper and more mature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for upgradability / retrofit timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Aircraft/battery system design should allow updating to newer chemistries; retro-fit of Boeing 787 battery reported to take ~two years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design flexibility reduces obsolescence risk. 'It is advisable that aircraft manufacturers design planes that allow updating to more advanced technologies as better batteries become available.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational/public-safety/regulatory risk
rubrics_metrics.description: A single safety breach can have severe public perception and regulatory consequences (FAA grounding); technology maturity must meet aviation certification expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two incidents on a new airplane hint at a design flaw; manufacturers must prioritize safety maturity. Regulatory agencies may require containment strategies and conservative operational limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firefighting and in-situ mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical considerations for extinguishing or mitigating burning Li-ion batteries onboard (difficult to extinguish, specialized agents, potential requirement to allow burn-out).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flaming Li-ion is difficult to extinguish; airport firefighters used Halotron. If possible remove burning battery from flammables and use water to cool surroundings; in aircraft, removing battery isn't possible, so design must prevent spread or allow safe burn-out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application suitability and system-level tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Match battery chemistry and pack design to application priorities (weight, maintenance, capacity, safety); e.g., Li-ion chosen for lower weight and low maintenance but NiCd offers robustness/maturity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Dreamliner needed extra capacity and lower maintenance, motivating Li-ion selection. Consider tradeoffs: NiCd doubles weight/number of cells but is well-understood; Li-ion offers higher energy but may require additional safety measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hidden/omitted battery attributes to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond spider-web basic attributes, consider toxicity, internal resistance, charge acceptance at cold temps, capacity loss during storage, self-discharge, and safety when abused or aged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes spider webs 'omit other important features' — include these dimensions in any evaluation matrix and testing program.
